status_summary: On 2025-02-05 the Attorney General issued department-wide memoranda on immigration enforcement. The charging policy memorandum has an immigration section that directs U.S. Attorney's Offices and other components to pursue criminal immigration-related charges that law enforcement agencies present, where the evidence supports them, and to investigate state and local actors who obstruct lawful immigration-related commands, requires an urgent report for any declination and requires each office to report quarterly statistics to the Executive Office for U.S. Attorneys. The 'Sanctuary Jurisdiction Directives' memorandum on justice.gov directs the Department to keep funds from jurisdictions that refuse to comply with 8 U.S.C. 1373, refuse to certify compliance or willfully fail to follow other federal immigration laws, directs U.S. Attorney's Offices and litigating components to investigate and, where the evidence supports it, prosecute violations of 18 U.S.C. 371 and 8 U.S.C. 1324 and 1373, directs the Civil Division to challenge state and local laws that impede federal operations, and restricts funding agreements with nongovernmental organizations that support removable aliens; it does not address obtaining criminal-alien information as such, and its nearest provision is the 8 U.S.C. 1373 information-sharing requirement. Executive Order 14159 (signed 2025-01-20) directs the Attorney General to prioritize prosecution of unauthorized entry and presence, and Executive Order 14287 (signed 2025-04-28) directs the Attorney General and the Homeland Security Secretary to publish a list of jurisdictions it describes as obstructing enforcement, notify them and pursue legal remedies; DOJ published a list of 35 jurisdictions on 2025-08-05 and the Attorney General's letter of 2025-08-13 to California's governor warned that officials could face prosecution (per press coverage). The U.S. Sentencing Commission reports that 22,743 of 66,662 federal cases in fiscal year 2025 involved immigration offenses and that reentry-after-removal offenses rose 45 percent from the prior year. The litigation route has not succeeded in the cases found: federal judges dismissed DOJ suits against Illinois and Chicago (2025-07-25; DOJ later said it would appeal to the Seventh Circuit, reported 2025-10-24), Los Angeles (reported 2026-06-23) and Minnesota with Minneapolis, St. Paul and Hennepin County (2026-07-20), per press reports. No DOJ step that has obtained criminal-alien information from sanctuary jurisdictions beyond these memoranda, notices and suits was found.

timeline.event: Executive Order 14159 directs the Attorney General to prioritize prosecuting unauthorized entry and presence (section 5) and, with the Homeland Security Secretary, to act to keep sanctuary jurisdictions from receiving federal funds and to evaluate other lawful actions (section 17); published 2025-01-29 at 90 FR 8443.

The Attorney General issues department-wide memoranda. The 'Sanctuary Jurisdiction Directives' memorandum directs a pause and review of DOJ funds to sanctuary jurisdictions, 8 U.S.C. 1373(a) compliance for grants, investigation and prosecution of related offenses (18 U.S.C. 371, 8 U.S.C. 1324 and 1373), civil challenges to state and local laws that impede federal immigration operations, and limits on funding agreements with nongovernmental organizations that support removable aliens. A separate charging memorandum (General Policy Regarding Charging, Plea Negotiations, and Sentencing, section IV) directs U.S. Attorney's Offices to pursue criminal immigration-related charges presented by law enforcement where the evidence supports them, with urgent reports on declinations and quarterly reporting to EOUSA.

Executive Order 14287 directs the Attorney General and the Homeland Security Secretary to publish and update a list of jurisdictions it describes as obstructing immigration enforcement, notify each, and pursue legal remedies against those that persist (published 2025-05-02 at 90 FR 18761). It has no provision on obtaining criminal-alien information from those jurisdictions.

U.S. District Judge Lindsay Jenkins (N.D. Ill.) dismisses the DOJ suit against Illinois and Chicago, rejecting DOJ's preemption argument and writing that the federal government cannot use intergovernmental immunity to commandeer states, which she described as barred by the Tenth Amendment (per press report).

DOJ publishes its list of 35 sanctuary jurisdictions (12 states, the District of Columbia, four counties and 18 cities), as the April 2025 order required. On 2025-08-13 the Attorney General wrote to California's governor that officials who obstruct immigration enforcement could be prosecuted, and stated that she had directed all U.S. Attorney's offices to investigate possible violations of federal immigration law by state or local governments (letter reported 2025-08-15 by Police1).

The U.S. Sentencing Commission's fact sheet on reentry offenses for fiscal year 2025 (page last modified 2026-05-04) reports 22,743 immigration cases among 66,662 federal cases, and a 45% rise in reentry-after-removal offenses from the prior year.

Judge Fernando Olguin dismisses the DOJ suit over Los Angeles's sanctuary ordinance, finding the allegations insufficient on intergovernmental immunity; the report is dated 2026-06-23 and says the ruling came over the preceding weekend, and the administration had until 2026-07-03 to file an amended complaint (per press report).

Chief Judge Eric Tostrud dismisses the DOJ suits against Minnesota and ordinances in Minneapolis, St. Paul and Hennepin County; the report gives no reasoning and says the Justice Department had to decide whether to appeal (per press report).
